blocks.text: Ampere's circuital law

The Biot–Savart law gives the field of any current, but the sums (integrals) can be long. When a current distribution is highly symmetric, a second law, **Ampere's circuital law**, gives the field in a few lines. It plays the same role in magnetism that Gauss's law plays in electrostatics.

**The line integral of B.** Take any closed path in space and choose a direction in which to go round it. Divide the path into small vector elements $d\vec{l}$ pointing along that direction. For each element form $\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B\,dl\cos\theta$, which picks out the part of $\vec{B}$ that lies along the path. Adding these products all the way round gives the **line integral** (or circulation) of $\vec{B}$, written $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}$.

$\vec{B}$ = magnetic field on the path (T); $d\vec{l}$ = small element of the closed path (m); $I_{\text{enc}}$ = net current (A) crossing any surface bounded by the path; $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$. The left side has units T m.
The line integral of the magnetic field around any closed path in vacuum equals $\mu_0$ times the net steady current threading (passing through) that path.
The imaginary closed path chosen for applying Ampere's law. It need not be a real wire or a circle; it is chosen to match the symmetry of the current so that the line integral is easy to evaluate.

**Sign of the current.** Curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction in which you go round the loop; currents along your thumb count as positive and currents in the opposite direction count as negative.

**Only enclosed current counts.** A current outside the loop does produce a field at points on the loop, but its contributions to $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}$ add up to zero over the complete loop. So the line integral can be zero even where $\vec{B}$ is not zero.

**Validity.** In this form the law holds for steady (time-independent) currents; Maxwell later added a term for changing electric fields. For steady currents it is equivalent to the Biot–Savart law, but it is only *useful* for finding $B$ when symmetry lets us take $B$ outside the integral.

**Choosing the Amperian loop.** Pick a path made of pieces on which one of these is true:
1. $\vec{B}$ is tangential to the path and has the same magnitude everywhere on it, so that piece gives $B\times(\text{its length})$;
2. $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the path, so that piece gives zero;
3. $\vec{B}$ is zero on that piece, so it gives zero.

Three long parallel wires pass through a closed loop: 6 A upward, 2 A downward and 5 A upward, and a fourth wire carrying 10 A lies outside the loop. Going round the loop so that 'upward' is positive, $I_{\text{enc}} = 6 - 2 + 5 = 9\,\text{A}$ and $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0\times9 = 1.13\times10^{-5}\,\text{T m}$. The 10 A wire changes the field on the loop but not the value of the line integral.

Ampere's law: $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}$. Only the net current threading the loop appears on the right, with signs fixed by the right-hand rule. The law is always true for steady currents, but it gives $B$ easily only for symmetric cases: the long straight wire, the long solenoid and the toroid.
Field of an infinitely long straight wire

Consider a very long (ideally infinite) straight wire carrying a steady current $I$. We want $B$ at a point P at perpendicular distance $r$ from the wire.

**Symmetry.** Rotating the wire about its own axis, or sliding it along its length, changes nothing. So $B$ can depend only on $r$, and the field lines must be circles centred on the wire (as Oersted's iron filings show). At every point of such a circle $\vec{B}$ is tangential and has the same magnitude.

**Amperian loop.** Choose the circle of radius $r$ through P, centred on the wire and lying in a plane perpendicular to it. Going round in the direction of $\vec{B}$, $\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B\,dl$ everywhere, so
$$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = B\oint dl = B\,(2\pi r)$$
The current threading the circle is $I$. Ampere's law gives $B\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I$.

Field of an infinitely long straight wire at perpendicular distance $r$ (m), current $I$ (A). In numbers, $B = 2\times10^{-7}\,I/r$ tesla. The field lines are circles round the wire; their sense is given by the right-hand thumb rule (thumb along the current, fingers along $\vec{B}$).

**Features of the result.**
- $B \propto I$ and $B \propto 1/r$: doubling the distance halves the field (compare the $1/r^2$ field of a single current element).
- Outside the wire the result does not depend on the thickness of the wire, only on the total current.
- The Biot–Savart law gives the same answer after integration along the wire, which confirms that the two laws agree.

**Inside a thick wire.** Let the wire have radius $a$ with the current spread uniformly over its cross-section. For an Amperian circle of radius $r < a$, only the fraction $\pi r^2/\pi a^2$ of the current is enclosed:
$$B\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\,\frac{r^2}{a^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad B = \frac{\mu_0 I\,r}{2\pi a^2}\quad (r < a)$$
So $B$ rises linearly from zero on the axis to its maximum value $\mu_0 I/2\pi a$ at the surface, and then falls as $1/r$ outside, as the graph shows.

For a straight wire of finite length, the Biot–Savart law gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\phi_1 + \sin\phi_2)$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance and $\phi_1, \phi_2$ are the angles the two ends subtend at the point, measured from the perpendicular. For an infinite wire $\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 90^\circ$ and this becomes $\mu_0 I/2\pi d$; at a point opposite one end of a very long (semi-infinite) wire it is half of that, $\mu_0 I/4\pi d$.

blocks.problem: A long vertical wire carries a current of 12 A upwards. Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at a point 6.0 cm due east of the wire.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: Magnitude from Ampere's law for a long straight wire, with the distance in metres: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times12}{0.06} = 4.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$.

Step 2: Direction from the right-hand thumb rule. Point the thumb upward along the current; seen from above, the fingers curl anticlockwise. At a point east of the wire, anticlockwise motion (seen from above) is towards the north.

Check with vectors: the current is along $+\hat{k}$ (up) and the point is along $+\hat{i}$ (east), so $\vec{B}$ is along $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$, which is north.

blocks.problem: A long straight copper rod of radius 2.0 mm carries a current of 10 A distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Find the magnetic field (a) 1.0 mm from the axis, (b) at the surface, (c) 4.0 mm from the axis.
blocks.solution:
(a) The point is inside the rod, so only part of the current is enclosed: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2} = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times10\times(1.0\times10^{-3})}{(2.0\times10^{-3})^2} = \frac{2\times10^{-9}}{4\times10^{-6}} = 5.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

(b) At the surface the whole current is enclosed: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times10}{2.0\times10^{-3}} = 1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$, the largest value anywhere.

(c) Outside, the rod acts like a thin wire carrying the full current: $B = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times10}{4.0\times10^{-3}} = 5.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$. Notice that the field halfway to the axis equals the field at twice the radius.

blocks.text: Magnetic field of a long solenoid

**Derivation with Ampere's law.** Take the rectangular Amperian loop abcd shown in the figure: side ab (length $h$) inside the solenoid parallel to the axis, side cd outside, and sides bc and da perpendicular to the axis.
- Along ab: $\vec{B}$ is uniform and parallel to the path, contribution $Bh$.
- Along bc and da: inside the solenoid $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to these sides, and outside it is zero, so they contribute nothing.
- Along cd: the field outside is zero, so the contribution is zero.

Hence $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = Bh$. The loop is crossed by $nh$ turns, each carrying $I$, so $I_{\text{enc}} = nhI$. Ampere's law gives $Bh = \mu_0 n h I$.

Field inside a long solenoid. $n = N/L$ = number of turns per unit length ($\text{m}^{-1}$), $N$ = total number of turns, $L$ = length (m), $I$ = current (A). The field is the same at every inside point away from the ends and does not depend on the radius of the solenoid.

**Further results and uses.**
- **At the ends** of a long solenoid (on the axis) the field is $\mu_0 n I/2$, half the central value, because the solenoid now extends on one side of the point only.
- **Polarity:** look at an end of the solenoid. If the current there appears anticlockwise, that end is a north pole; if clockwise, a south pole. Equivalently, curl the right-hand fingers along the current in the turns and the thumb points along $\vec{B}$ inside, towards the north end.
- **With a core:** filling the solenoid with a material of relative permeability $\mu_r$ (for example soft iron) multiplies the field: $B = \mu_0\mu_r n I$. This is the principle of the electromagnet.
- Solenoids are used wherever a uniform, controllable magnetic field is needed: electromagnets, relays, MRI magnets, and in experiments on charged particles.

A **toroid** is a solenoid bent into a closed ring. With $N$ turns and current $I$, an Amperian circle of radius $r$ inside the core gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$; the field is zero in the open space inside the ring and outside the toroid. If the ring is large, $N/2\pi r = n$ and the result becomes $\mu_0 n I$, the same as for a straight solenoid.

blocks.problem: A solenoid 60 cm long has 1200 turns and carries a current of 2.0 A. Find the magnetic field (a) inside it near the middle, (b) at its ends on the axis. (c) What current would give a central field of 0.010 T?
blocks.solution:
Step 1: Turns per unit length: $n = N/L = 1200/0.60 = 2000\,\text{m}^{-1}$.

(a) Inside, away from the ends: $B = \mu_0 n I = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000\times2.0 = 5.03\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$.

(b) At either end the field is half the central value: $B_{\text{end}} = 2.51\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$.

(c) The field is proportional to the current, so rearrange $B = \mu_0 n I$: $I = \frac{B}{\mu_0 n} = \frac{0.010}{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000} = \frac{0.010}{2.513\times10^{-3}} = 3.98\,\text{A}$, that is about 4.0 A.

blocks.text: Force on a moving charge in a uniform magnetic field

A charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ through a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ experiences the **magnetic Lorentz force**. Its magnitude is $qvB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$, and its direction is perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$.

$q$ = charge with sign (C), $\vec{v}$ = velocity ($\text{m s}^{-1}$), $\vec{B}$ = magnetic field (T). For a positive charge the force is along $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ (right-hand rule); for a negative charge such as an electron it is opposite. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the same result: forefinger along $\vec{B}$, middle finger along the conventional current (the velocity of a positive charge), thumb along the force.

**Properties of the magnetic force.**
- It is zero if the charge is at rest ($v = 0$), or moves parallel or antiparallel to $\vec{B}$ ($\sin\theta = 0$).
- It is maximum, $qvB$, when $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.
- It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it **does no work**. It can change the direction of motion but not the speed or kinetic energy of the particle.

**Case 1: velocity parallel to B.** No force acts, and the particle moves in a straight line with constant velocity.

**Case 2: velocity perpendicular to B.** The force has constant magnitude $qvB$ and is always at right angles to the velocity, exactly what is needed for uniform circular motion. The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:
$$qvB = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$
The time for one revolution is $T = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi m/qB$. It does **not** depend on the speed or the radius: a faster particle moves on a proportionally larger circle and takes the same time. The corresponding frequency is called the cyclotron frequency.

$m$ = mass (kg), $v$ = speed ($\text{m s}^{-1}$), $p = mv$ = momentum, $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ = kinetic energy (J), $r$ = radius (m), $T$ = period (s), $\nu$ = frequency (Hz), $\omega$ = angular frequency ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$). Valid for $\vec{v}$ perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ and speeds much less than that of light.

**Sense of rotation.** In panel (a) the field points into the page. At the bottom of the circle the positive charge moves to the right, and $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ points up, towards the centre, so the charge goes round anticlockwise. An electron in the same field goes round clockwise.

**Case 3: velocity at an angle θ to B.** Split the velocity into $v_\parallel = v\cos\theta$ along $\vec{B}$ and $v_\perp = v\sin\theta$ perpendicular to it. The parallel part feels no force and stays constant; the perpendicular part produces circular motion. The combination is a **helix** whose axis is along $\vec{B}$, as in panel (b). The distance moved along the field in one revolution is the **pitch**.

blocks.latex: r = \frac{m v\sin\theta}{qB}, \qquad p = v\cos\theta\times T = \frac{2\pi m\,v\cos\theta}{qB}
blocks.text: Radius $r$ and pitch $p$ of the helical path (both in m). $\theta$ = angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. The period $T = 2\pi m/qB$ is unchanged by the parallel motion.

blocks.problem: An electron moving at $3.0\times10^{7}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of $6.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$ at right angles to the field. Find the radius of its path and its frequency of revolution. ($m_e = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg}$, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$)
blocks.solution:
Step 1: The velocity is perpendicular to the field, so the electron moves in a circle whose centripetal force is the magnetic force. Radius: $r = \frac{mv}{eB} = \frac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times3.0\times10^{7}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times6.0\times10^{-4}} = \frac{2.73\times10^{-23}}{9.6\times10^{-23}} = 0.284\,\text{m}$.

Step 2: Frequency, which does not depend on the speed: $\nu = \frac{eB}{2\pi m} = \frac{1.6\times10^{-19}\times6.0\times10^{-4}}{2\pi\times9.1\times10^{-31}} = \frac{9.6\times10^{-23}}{5.72\times10^{-30}} = 1.68\times10^{7}\,\text{Hz}$.

Step 3: The period is the reciprocal, $T = 1/\nu = 5.96\times10^{-8}\,\text{s}$.

blocks.problem: A proton moving at $2.0\times10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T with its velocity at $60^\circ$ to the field. Find the radius and pitch of its helical path. ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$)
blocks.solution:
Step 1: Resolve the velocity. Perpendicular part $v_\perp = v\sin60^\circ = 1.732\times10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$; parallel part $v_\parallel = v\cos60^\circ = 1.0\times10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: Radius from the perpendicular part only: $r = \frac{m v_\perp}{eB} = \frac{1.67\times10^{-27}\times1.732\times10^{6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.10} = \frac{2.89\times10^{-21}}{1.6\times10^{-20}} = 0.181\,\text{m}$.

Step 3: Period: $T = \frac{2\pi m}{eB} = \frac{2\pi\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{1.6\times10^{-20}} = 6.56\times10^{-7}\,\text{s}$.

Step 4: Pitch, the distance travelled along the field in one period: $p = v_\parallel T = 1.0\times10^{6}\times6.56\times10^{-7} = 0.656\,\text{m}$.
blocks.answer: Radius about 18 cm; pitch about 66 cm

blocks.text:
**Common mistakes.**
- Using $v$ instead of $v\sin\theta$ for the radius, or $v$ instead of $v\cos\theta$ for the pitch of a helix.
- Forgetting that the force on an electron is opposite to $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$.
- Thinking a magnetic field can speed a particle up. It cannot; only an electric field changes the kinetic energy.
- For particles with the same kinetic energy, use $r = \sqrt{2mK}/qB$: a proton and an alpha particle ($4m$, $2e$) then have equal radii.
Force on a moving charge in uniform electric and magnetic fields

When both an electric field $\vec{E}$ and a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ are present, the total force on a charge is the sum of the electric force $q\vec{E}$ and the magnetic force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$. This total is called the **Lorentz force**.

$\vec{E}$ = electric field ($\text{V m}^{-1}$ or $\text{N C}^{-1}$), $\vec{B}$ = magnetic field (T), $\vec{v}$ = velocity of the charge, $q$ = charge. The electric part acts whether or not the charge moves; the magnetic part acts only on a moving charge.

**Motion in a uniform electric field alone.** The force $q\vec{E}$ is constant, so the acceleration $a = qE/m$ is constant. A charge entering the field with velocity $v$ perpendicular to $\vec{E}$ behaves like a projectile: it keeps its speed $v$ across the field and accelerates along it. After moving a distance $x$ across the field it has been deflected by
$$y = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{qE}{m}\left(\frac{x}{v}\right)^2 = \frac{qE\,x^2}{2mv^2}$$
so its path is a **parabola**. The electric force does work and changes the speed.

**Crossed fields: the velocity selector.** Let $\vec{E}$, $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{v}$ be mutually perpendicular, arranged so that the electric and magnetic forces on the charge point in opposite directions (see the figure). The electric force $qE$ is the same for every particle, but the magnetic force $qvB$ grows with speed. The particle goes straight through when the two forces balance:
$$qE = qvB \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \frac{E}{B}$$
Faster particles ($v > E/B$) are pushed to the side of the magnetic force, slower ones to the side of the electric force, and both are stopped by the exit slit. The selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass, so the same setting passes protons, electrons or ions that have this speed. J. J. Thomson used crossed fields in measuring $e/m$ for the electron, and velocity selectors are used in mass spectrometers.
Speed of the particles that pass undeflected through crossed uniform fields ($\vec{E}\perp\vec{B}\perp\vec{v}$). $E$ in $\text{V m}^{-1}$, $B$ in T, $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

blocks.problem: In a velocity selector the electric field is $3.0\times10^{4}\,\text{V m}^{-1}$ and the magnetic field is 0.020 T, at right angles to each other. (a) What speed do undeflected particles have? (b) If the electric field is switched off, what is the radius of the circle in which a proton of this speed moves? ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$)
blocks.solution:
(a) For no deflection the electric and magnetic forces must balance, $qE = qvB$, so $v = \frac{E}{B} = \frac{3.0\times10^{4}}{0.020} = 1.5\times10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. This holds for any charge and any mass.

(b) With only the magnetic field left, the proton moves in a circle with the magnetic force providing the centripetal force: $r = \frac{mv}{eB} = \frac{1.67\times10^{-27}\times1.5\times10^{6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.020} = \frac{2.505\times10^{-21}}{3.2\times10^{-21}} = 0.78\,\text{m}$.

blocks.text: Lorentz force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. The electric force changes speed; the magnetic force only changes direction. In a magnetic field: parallel motion gives a straight line, perpendicular motion a circle ($r = mv/qB$, $T = 2\pi m/qB$), oblique motion a helix. In crossed fields only particles with $v = E/B$ pass undeflected, whatever their charge or mass.
Summary and exam strategy

blocks.caption: Formula sheet
rows: Inside a thick wire ($r < a$, uniform current)
$B = \mu_0 n I$ (end of axis: $\mu_0 n I/2$)

blocks.text:
**Exam shortcuts.**
- $\mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}$, so for a straight wire $B = 2\times10^{-7}I/r$.
- Two parallel wires with **opposite** currents: fields **add** at points between them. With currents in the **same** direction the fields cancel at the midpoint (for equal currents).
- For a solenoid made from a fixed length of wire on a fixed length, a larger radius means fewer turns and a weaker field.
- When a question asks whether a particle 'gains energy' in a magnetic field, the answer is always no.

Revision checklist: state Ampere's law and the sign rule; derive $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi r$ for a long wire and $B = \mu_0 n I$ for a solenoid using a suitable Amperian loop; write the magnetic and Lorentz forces with directions; obtain $r$, $T$ and pitch for charged particles; explain the velocity selector condition $v = E/B$.

questions.stem: According to Ampere's circuital law, the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop depends on
options: all the currents near the loop, whether inside or outside it
the shape and size of the loop
only the net current threading the loop
the magnetic field at the centre of the loop
questions.explanation: Ampere's law states that the line integral of B around any closed path equals mu-nought times the net current passing through the path. Currents outside the loop change the field on the loop but contribute zero in total to the line integral, and the shape of the loop does not matter.

optionRationale.1: Outside currents do produce field on the loop, but their net contribution to the line integral is zero.
optionRationale.2: Any loop enclosing the same net current gives the same line integral, whatever its shape or size.
optionRationale.4: The law relates the integral to the enclosed current, not to the field at any single point.

questions.objective: State Ampere's circuital law

questions.stem: Two long wires pass through a closed loop: one carries 5 A upward and the other 3 A downward. A third wire carrying 4 A upward lies outside the loop. The loop is traversed so that upward current counts as positive. What is the value of the line integral of B around the loop? (Take $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$.)
questions.explanation: Only the currents that thread the loop count, with signs. The enclosed current is 5 A minus 3 A, which is 2 A; the 4 A wire is outside and contributes nothing. So the line integral is $\mu_0\times2 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2 = 2.5\times10^{-6}\,\text{T m}$.

optionRationale.2: This wrongly includes the 4 A wire that lies outside the loop (net 6 A).
optionRationale.3: This adds the two enclosed currents (8 A) and ignores that they flow in opposite directions.
optionRationale.4: This adds all three currents (12 A) without signs.

questions.objective: Apply the sign convention for enclosed current in Ampere's law

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop can be zero even though the magnetic field is not zero at any point of the loop.
Reason (R): Ampere's law relates the line integral only to the net current enclosed; a current outside the loop produces a field on it but its contributions to the line integral add up to zero.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: If a loop encloses no net current but lies near a current-carrying wire outside it, the field at every point of the loop is non-zero. Yet the line integral is zero, because on parts of the loop the field is along the path and on other parts against it, and these cancel. This is exactly what R states, so R explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is precisely the reason why the integral vanishes while B does not, so it does explain A.
optionRationale.3: R is a correct statement of what Ampere's law says about outside currents.
optionRationale.4: A is true: a zero line integral does not require a zero field.

questions.objective: Distinguish between zero circulation and zero field

questions.stem: What is the magnetic field at a distance of 5 cm from a long straight wire carrying a current of 10 A?
questions.explanation: For a long straight wire, Ampere's law applied to a circle of radius r round the wire gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. Converting the distance to metres (5 cm = 0.05 m) and using $\mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}$: $B = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times10}{0.05} = 4\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$, directed along the circle through the point.

optionRationale.1: This uses $\mu_0/4\pi$ instead of $\mu_0/2\pi$, giving half the correct value.
optionRationale.3: This uses the circular-loop formula $\mu_0 I/2r$, which does not apply to a straight wire.
optionRationale.4: This uses 5 m instead of 0.05 m for the distance.

questions.objective: Calculate the field of a long straight wire

questions.stem: A long vertical wire carries a current upwards. In which direction is the magnetic field at a point due east of the wire?
options: Towards the east, away from the wire
questions.explanation: Point the right thumb up along the current; seen from above, the fingers curl anticlockwise round the wire. At a point to the east, anticlockwise circulation is directed north. With vectors, the field is along the current direction crossed with the outward direction, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$, which is north.

optionRationale.1: South would be correct for a downward current.
optionRationale.2: The field of a straight wire is tangential to circles round the wire, never radial.
optionRationale.4: The field is perpendicular to the wire, so it cannot be vertical here.

questions.objective: Find the direction of the field of a straight wire with the right-hand thumb rule

questions.stem: A long cylindrical wire of radius $a$ carries a current distributed uniformly over its cross-section. What is the ratio of the magnetic field at distance $a/2$ from the axis to the field at distance $2a$ from the axis?
questions.explanation: Inside the wire an Amperian circle of radius r encloses only the fraction of current inside it, which gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}$; at $r = a/2$ this is $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}$. Outside, the whole current is enclosed and $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; at $r = 2a$ this is also $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}$. The two fields are equal, so the ratio is one to one.

optionRationale.1: This treats both points as if the field varied as $1/r$ everywhere, forgetting that inside the wire only part of the current is enclosed.
optionRationale.2: This reverses a wrong ratio; the field inside rises with r, so it is not larger at a/2.
optionRationale.3: This assumes $B \propto r^2$ inside, which is not the result of Ampere's law.

questions.objective: Apply Ampere's law inside and outside a thick wire

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires are 10 cm apart and carry currents of 5 A each in opposite directions. What is the magnetic field at the point midway between them?
questions.explanation: Each wire is 5 cm from the midpoint and gives $B = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\times5}{0.05} = 2\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$. With opposite currents, the right-hand rule shows that the two fields point the same way at points between the wires, so they add to give a total of four times ten to the minus five tesla.

optionRationale.2: The fields cancel at the midpoint only when the two equal currents flow in the same direction.
optionRationale.3: This is the field of just one wire.
optionRationale.4: This uses the full separation of 10 cm instead of 5 cm and also forgets to add the second wire.

questions.objective: Superpose the fields of two parallel wires

questions.stem: Panel (b) of the figure shows how B varies with distance r from the axis of a long cylindrical wire of radius a carrying a uniformly distributed current. Which statement does the graph correctly show?
options: The field is greatest on the axis of the wire
The field is greatest at the surface and falls as 1/r outside
The field is uniform everywhere inside the wire
The field outside depends on the radius a of the wire
questions.explanation: Inside, the enclosed current grows as the square of r, which makes B grow linearly from zero on the axis. Outside, all the current is enclosed and B falls as one over r. The two parts meet at the surface, where B reaches its maximum value of mu-nought I over two pi a.

optionRationale.1: On the axis no current is enclosed, so B is zero there.
optionRationale.3: B is proportional to r inside, not constant.
optionRationale.4: Outside, B depends only on the total current and the distance, not on the wire's radius.

questions.objective: Interpret the B versus r graph for a thick current-carrying wire

questions.stem: A solenoid of length 0.5 m has 500 turns and carries a current of 4 A. What is the magnetic field inside it, well away from the ends? (Take $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$.)
questions.explanation: First find the number of turns per metre: 500 turns divided by 0.5 m gives 1000 turns per metre. The field inside a long solenoid is then $B = \mu_0 n I = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times4 = 5.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$. This value is uniform throughout the inside of the solenoid away from its ends and is directed along the axis.

optionRationale.1: This is the field at the ends of the solenoid, half the central value.
optionRationale.2: This leaves out the current of 4 A.
optionRationale.4: This uses 2000 turns per metre, as if the length were 0.25 m.

questions.objective: Calculate the field inside a long solenoid

questions.stem: A long solenoid has $n$ turns per unit length and carries current $I$. What is the magnetic field at a point on its axis exactly at one end?
questions.explanation: At the end of a long solenoid, the turns lie on one side of the point only. By symmetry, the field there is half of what it would be if the solenoid extended equally on both sides, so it equals half of the central value, $\mu_0 n I/2$.

optionRationale.1: This is the field deep inside the solenoid, not at its end.
optionRationale.3: The field at the end is smaller, not larger, than the central field.
optionRationale.4: The field drops to zero only far outside; at the end it is still half the central value.

questions.objective: Recall the field at the end of a long solenoid

questions.stem:
Consider these statements about the magnetic field of a long, closely wound solenoid:
A. The field inside is uniform and parallel to the axis.
B. The field outside is nearly zero.
C. The field inside increases if the radius of the solenoid is increased, other things remaining the same.
D. The field inside becomes four times as large if both the number of turns per unit length and the current are doubled.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Ampere's law gives $B = \mu_0 n I$ inside, uniform and along the axis, with a negligible field outside, so A and B are true. The radius does not appear in this result, so C is false. Doubling both n and I multiplies B by two times two, which is four, so D is true.

optionRationale.1: Leaves out D, which follows directly from B = mu0 n I.
optionRationale.2: C is false; the field of a long solenoid does not depend on its radius.
optionRationale.3: Includes the false statement C and leaves out the true statements A and B.

questions.objective: Analyse the properties of the field of a long solenoid

questions.stem: A fixed length of insulated wire is wound uniformly over the whole length L of a cylindrical tube to make a long solenoid. It is then unwound and rewound uniformly over the same length L on a tube of twice the radius. With the same current, how does the field inside change?
questions.explanation: Each turn now needs twice as much wire, so the fixed length of wire makes only half as many turns. Since the length L is unchanged, the number of turns per unit length n is halved. The field inside a long solenoid is mu-nought n I and does not depend on the radius, so it is halved.

optionRationale.2: A larger radius gives fewer turns, so the field cannot increase.
optionRationale.3: The field does not depend on radius directly, but the number of turns per unit length changes here.
optionRationale.4: Only n changes, and only by a factor of two, so the field becomes half, not one-quarter.

questions.objective: Reason how solenoid dimensions affect turns per unit length and the field

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The magnetic field inside a long solenoid does not depend on the radius of the solenoid.
Reason (R): The magnetic field at the centre of a single circular loop is inversely proportional to its radius.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A is true: Ampere's law gives $B = \mu_0 n I$ with no radius in it. R is also true: for one loop $B = \mu_0 I/2R$. But R does not explain A; the radius-independence of the solenoid field comes from applying Ampere's law to a rectangular loop, not from the single-loop formula, which on its own would suggest the opposite.

optionRationale.1: R is true but is not the reason the solenoid field is independent of radius.
optionRationale.3: R is a correct result of the Biot–Savart law.
optionRationale.4: A is true, as B = mu0 n I shows.

questions.objective: Connect the solenoid field formula with its derivation

questions.stem: A charged particle moves through a region containing only a uniform magnetic field. What is the work done on it by the magnetic force?
options: Positive if the particle is positively charged
Equal to qvB multiplied by the distance moved
Negative if the particle moves against the field
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$, which is always perpendicular to the velocity, and therefore to every small displacement. A force perpendicular to the displacement does no work, so the speed and the kinetic energy of the particle stay constant; only the direction of motion changes.

optionRationale.1: The sign of the charge changes the direction of the force, but the force stays perpendicular to the motion.
optionRationale.2: qvB is the size of the force, but it never acts along the displacement.
optionRationale.3: Even when moving against the field the magnetic force has no component along the motion.

questions.objective: Recognise that a magnetic force does no work

questions.stem: A proton and an alpha particle have the same kinetic energy and enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles to it. What is the ratio of the radius of the proton's path to that of the alpha particle's path?
questions.explanation: With kinetic energy K, the momentum is $\sqrt{2mK}$, so $r = \frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$. The alpha particle has four times the mass and twice the charge of the proton. Its radius has the factor $\sqrt{4}/2 = 1$ relative to the proton, so the two radii are equal and the ratio is one to one.

optionRationale.1: This would follow if both particles had the same speed and the ratio were inverted; it ignores the kinetic-energy condition.
optionRationale.2: This is the alpha-to-proton ratio for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.
optionRationale.4: This includes the mass factor but forgets the double charge of the alpha particle.

questions.objective: Compare radii of charged particles with equal kinetic energy

questions.stem: An electron moving at $2.0\times10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of $1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{T}$ at right angles to it. What is the radius of its circular path? ($m_e = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg}$, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$)
questions.explanation: Because the electron enters at right angles to the field, it moves in a circle and the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, $evB = mv^2/r$. Solving for the radius: $r = \frac{mv}{eB} = \frac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times2.0\times10^{6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times1.0\times10^{-3}} = \frac{1.82\times10^{-24}}{1.6\times10^{-22}} = 1.14\times10^{-2}\,\text{m}$, which is about 1.14 centimetres.

optionRationale.1: This is half the correct radius, as if the speed had been halved.
optionRationale.3: This is the diameter of the circle, not its radius.
optionRationale.4: This is ten times too large, an error in the power of ten.

questions.objective: Calculate the radius of a charged particle's circular path

questions.stem: Panel (a) of the figure shows a positive charge going round anticlockwise in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. If the field is reversed so that it points out of the page and the speed of the charge is doubled, how does the motion change?
questions.explanation: Reversing the field reverses the force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$, so the charge now goes round clockwise. The radius $r = mv/qB$ is proportional to the speed, so it doubles. The period $T = 2\pi m/qB$ does not involve the speed, so it stays the same.

optionRationale.1: Reversing B must reverse the sense of rotation, and the period does not depend on speed.
optionRationale.3: A faster particle moves on a larger circle, not a smaller one.
optionRationale.4: The radius grows with speed while the period stays fixed, not the other way round.

questions.objective: Predict how direction of B and speed affect circular motion

questions.stem: A proton moving at $4.0\times10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T with its velocity at $60^\circ$ to the field. What is the pitch of its helical path? ($m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$)
questions.explanation: First find the time for one revolution, which depends only on the mass, charge and field: $T = \frac{2\pi m}{eB} = \frac{2\pi\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.20} = 3.28\times10^{-7}\,\text{s}$. The component of velocity along the field is $v\cos60^\circ = 2.0\times10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. The pitch is the distance travelled along the field in one period: $2.0\times10^{5}\times3.28\times10^{-7} = 0.066\,\text{m}$, which is about 6.6 cm.

optionRationale.1: This leaves out the factor $2\pi$ in the period.
optionRationale.2: This uses $v\sin60^\circ$, the perpendicular component, instead of $v\cos60^\circ$.
optionRationale.3: This uses the full speed instead of the component along the field.

questions.objective: Calculate the pitch of a helical path

questions.stem: In the figure of the long solenoid, which sides of the rectangular Amperian loop abcd give a non-zero contribution to the line integral of B?
questions.explanation: Inside the solenoid the field is uniform and parallel to ab, so ab contributes B times h. Sides bc and da are perpendicular to the field inside and lie in a zero-field region outside, so they contribute nothing. Side cd is entirely outside, where the field is practically zero.

optionRationale.2: Side cd lies outside the solenoid, where the field is nearly zero.
optionRationale.3: These sides are perpendicular to B inside, so B dot dl is zero on them.
optionRationale.4: Three of the four sides contribute nothing, which is why the loop is chosen this way.

questions.objective: Evaluate the line integral for the solenoid's Amperian loop

questions.stem: In a velocity selector, the electric field is $6.0\times10^{4}\,\text{V m}^{-1}$ and the perpendicular magnetic field is 0.30 T. What speed must a charged particle have to pass straight through?
questions.explanation: In crossed fields the particle is undeflected only when the electric force qE is exactly balanced by the magnetic force qvB acting in the opposite direction. This gives $v = E/B = \frac{6.0\times10^{4}}{0.30} = 2.0\times10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. The charge and the mass of the particle cancel out of this condition, so only the speed matters.

optionRationale.1: This multiplies E by B instead of dividing.
optionRationale.2: This divides B by E, the inverse of the correct ratio.
optionRationale.4: This is ten times too small, a slip in the power of ten.

questions.objective: Use the velocity-selector condition v = E/B

questions.stem: A beam of protons passes undeflected through a region of crossed uniform electric and magnetic fields. Which of the following, entering with the same velocity, will also pass undeflected?
options: Only particles with the same charge-to-mass ratio as the proton
Any charged particle with the same velocity, whatever its charge or mass
questions.explanation: The condition for no deflection is qE = qvB, so v = E/B. The charge cancels and the mass never appears, because both forces are balanced at the instant of entry and stay balanced. Electrons, alpha particles or any ions with the same velocity also pass straight through, since both forces reverse together for negative charges.

optionRationale.1: Nothing in v = E/B is special to protons.
optionRationale.2: For a negative charge both forces reverse, so they still balance.
optionRationale.3: The mass and charge cancel completely; only the velocity matters.

questions.objective: Explain why a velocity selector depends only on speed

questions.stem: A proton moves with velocity $\vec{v} = 2.0\times10^{5}\,\hat{i}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B} = 0.50\,\hat{k}\,\text{T}$. What uniform electric field must be applied so that the net force on the proton is zero?
options: 1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ along the negative y-axis
1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ along the positive y-axis
4.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ along the positive y-axis
1.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ along the positive z-axis
questions.explanation: The net Lorentz force is zero when the electric force cancels the magnetic force, that is when $\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B} = 0$, so $\vec{E} = -\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$. Working out the cross product: $\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = (2.0\times10^{5})(0.50)(\hat{i}\times\hat{k}) = 1.0\times10^{5}(-\hat{j})$. Therefore the required field is $\vec{E} = +1.0\times10^{5}\,\hat{j}\,\text{V m}^{-1}$, a field of one hundred thousand volts per metre pointing along the positive y-axis.

optionRationale.1: This is the direction of $\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ itself; the electric field must be opposite to it.
optionRationale.3: This divides v by B instead of multiplying them.
optionRationale.4: An electric field along the magnetic field cannot cancel a magnetic force that lies along the y-axis.

questions.objective: Use the Lorentz force to find a balancing electric field

questions.stem: Match the situation of a charged particle in List-I with the shape of its path in List-II.

left: A. Velocity parallel to a uniform magnetic field
B. Velocity perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field
C. Velocity at an acute angle to a uniform magnetic field
D. Velocity perpendicular to a uniform electric field (no magnetic field)

questions.explanation: Parallel to B there is no magnetic force, so the path is straight (A-IV). Perpendicular to B, a constant force at right angles to the velocity gives a circle (B-III). At an angle, circular motion plus uniform drift along B gives a helix (C-I). A constant electric force across the motion gives a parabola, like a projectile (D-II).

optionRationale.1: Swaps the parallel and perpendicular cases; parallel motion feels no force at all.
optionRationale.2: Swaps circle and helix; the helix needs a velocity component along B.
optionRationale.4: A charge entering an electric field across its motion is deflected into a parabola, not a straight line.

questions.objective: Classify the paths of charged particles in uniform fields

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A charged particle projected into a uniform magnetic field always moves in a circle.
Reason (R): The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: R is true because the force is q times v cross B. But A is false: if the particle moves along the field it feels no force and goes straight, and if it enters at an angle it follows a helix. A circle results only when the velocity is perpendicular to the field.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so this cannot be correct.
optionRationale.2: A is false; the path is a circle only for perpendicular entry.
optionRationale.3: R is true; the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity.

questions.objective: Identify the conditions for circular motion in a magnetic field
